paras: The alleged lynching of a Swiss settler on Loup Creek was a claim, printed in German-language papers in 1880, that local whites in West Virginia's Kanawha Valley had threatened or lynched a Swiss immigrant for making his wife work. The man, identified as David Braun, was reported alive and prosperous in November 1880 and denied that any lynching had occurred. West Virginia papers treated the story as a slander meant to stop Swiss immigration to the state.

In 1880 Swiss commissioners, among them Kirchhoff and Brunner, backed a plan for a Swiss colony in the Kanawha Valley, buying land at a reported $7 an acre. The St. Louis Anzeiger des Westens opposed the plan, calling the region a rocky, wooded wilderness and urging settlers toward the prairie West instead. Braun had left Switzerland with a family of nine in December 1879 and arrived at Cotton Hill, Fayette County, on Loup Creek, later that month.

According to the Anzeiger des Westens, reprinted in Baltimore's Der Deutsche Correspondent on July 13, 1880, there was only one Swiss family in the whole valley, and the wife had to help with the heavy work "like a man." The paper said the local "poor white trash" first threatened to lynch the husband for daring to "force" a woman to such hard work, but that he fended them off and his wife kept working. When the article reached Switzerland through the New Yorker Staats-Zeitung and the Berner Post, it was summarized by Ludwig as charging that "the husband [was] lynched because he allowed his wife to work."

Em. D. Ludwig, a Swiss resident promoting immigration, answered in a letter to the Kanawha Gazette, saying that more than thirty Swiss families lived in the valley. He named the man as David Braun and said Braun had written to the Berner Post praising his neighbors and indignantly denying all charges of lynching. Ludwig listed Braun's livestock, crops and tobacco worth $1,000 to $1,500, calling him "the proudest, happiest little live Swiss in America."

The story began in German-language papers, where it served as an argument against Swiss settlement in West Virginia; Der Westbote of Columbus, Ohio, printed a rival German paper's defense of the colony without repeating the lynching charge. In November the Point Pleasant Weekly Register reprinted Ludwig's full letter, calling the Anzeiger's article an "infamous attack." The Wheeling Register ran extracts under the heading "Preventing Immigration to West Virginia," blaming the Republican campaign for putting the state "in bad repute even in Switzerland"; the Shepherdstown Register and the South Branch Intelligencer of Romney reprinted that item.

The accounts differ on what was claimed: the German original described only a threat to lynch, while Ludwig's English summary of a later reprint said the husband was lynched. They also differ on the reason, "forcing" his wife to work in the German text and "allowed his wife to work" in the English summary, and neither mentions beating. Braun's own denial, reported by Ludwig, is the only account from the man himself.

chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: The only episode in the coverage is a reported threat by local whites to lynch a Swiss immigrant for making his wife work, which the man himself later denied; no Black person is involved (A2, A6).

The original Anzeiger des Westens article reported only a threat to lynch, which the settler fended off (A2); a later summary of it said he was lynched (A5), but Ludwig reported the man, David Braun, alive, prosperous and denying any lynching (A6).
The St. Louis German paper's claim (A2, as summarized in A5) is denied by Ludwig and by Braun himself, who is reported alive (A6).

West Virginia papers printed Ludwig's denial under 'Preventing Immigration to West Virginia', treating the charge as a slander on the state with political motives.
